subject: pathology
title: CNS tumours: grading, types and locations

steps.tx: Brain tumours present by location rather than by systemic cancer symptoms. A **brain tumour** can cause seizures and focal deficits, and raised pressure causes **headache and vomiting** in many patients. Adult tumours favour supratentorial sites, childhood tumours favour the posterior fossa, and metastases outnumber primary tumours in adults.
steps.say: Tumours present by location because seizures and focal deficits reflect involved cortex. Raised intracranial pressure causes headache and vomiting in many affected patients. Adult tumours are supratentorial whereas childhood tumours are infratentorial more often. Metastases outnumber primary tumours because systemic cancers spread to brain.

steps.tx: Glioblastoma is the commonest malignant primary brain tumour in adults. **Glioblastoma** crosses the corpus callosum as a butterfly lesion, and **pseudopalisading necrosis** with microvascular proliferation defines grade four histology. Ring enhancement with central necrosis and oedema is characteristic on imaging, and IDH wild type tumours behave most aggressively.
steps.say: Glioblastoma is malignant and it crosses the corpus callosum between hemispheres. Ring enhancement is present because central necrosis develops inside the tumour mass. Pseudopalisading necrosis is characteristic and microvascular proliferation indicates grade four disease. IDH status is important because wild type tumours behave aggressively.

vis.alt: MRI showing glioblastoma butterfly lesion with ring enhancement, and histology showing pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation.
vis.caption: Glioblastoma: characteristic imaging and histological features

steps.tx: Meningioma is a slow growing tumour that arises from arachnoid cap cells. A **meningioma** compresses brain rather than invading it, and **psammoma bodies** with whorls are seen on histology. Dural tail enhancement and hyperostosis are imaging clues, and most tumours are benign and are cured by complete surgical excision.
steps.say: Meningioma arises from arachnoid cells and it grows slowly over years. Compression occurs without invasion because the tumour remains extra axial typically. Whorls and psammoma bodies are seen and progesterone receptors are expressed frequently. Excision is curative because most tumours are benign grade one lesions.

steps.tx: Medulloblastoma is an embryonal tumour of the cerebellar vermis in children. **Medulloblastoma** obstructs the fourth ventricle, and **Homer Wright rosettes** are formed by small blue embryonal cells. Spread occurs through cerebrospinal fluid to the spine, so staging images the whole neuraxis before treatment is planned for the child.
steps.say: Medulloblastoma is centred in the vermis and the fourth ventricle is obstructed in children. Small blue cells form rosettes and the tumour grows very rapidly clinically. Spinal seeding occurs because cells spread through cerebrospinal fluid pathways readily. Whole spine imaging is required because staging determines treatment intensity.

steps.tx: This MRI shows a midline cerebellar vermis mass with enhancing spinal nodules. The tumour is **medulloblastoma** with **spinal seeding** through cerebrospinal fluid, and the inset shows small blue cells around a Homer Wright rosette. Whole spine staging matters because drop metastases change treatment in this childhood tumour.
steps.say: This sagittal image is striking because a bright mass occupies the cerebellar vermis. Small enhancing nodules are present along the spinal canal from seeding. The inset is magnified and small blue cells with a rosette are visible. Spinal spread is important because staging changes treatment planning greatly.

vis.alt: Contrast enhanced sagittal head MRI with midline cerebellar mass and spinal nodules, plus histology inset.
vis.caption: Sagittal brain MRI showing cerebellar mass and spinal seeding. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Pituitary tumours present with hormone excess or with local mass effect. A **pituitary adenoma** can compress the optic chiasm, and **bitemporal hemianopia** results from that compression superiorly. Bleeding into a tumour causes apoplexy with headache and visual collapse, and lung, breast and melanoma are common sources of brain metastases.
steps.say: Pituitary tumours secrete hormones or they compress adjacent structures by expansion. The optic chiasm is compressed and temporal visual fields are lost bilaterally. Apoplexy occurs when bleeding develops inside an existing pituitary tumour suddenly. Steroids and urgent surgical opinion are required in that emergency.
